title: An undercover Google analyst infiltrated a notorious supply-chain hacking gang
gist: Google's threat intelligence group (via Mandiant) ran an undercover analyst inside TeamPCP, a supply-chain hacking group that compromised hundreds of open-source projects and over a thousand companies including GitHub, OpenAI and the European Commission, letting Google warn victims, disrupt an AI-generated zero-day 2FA bypass, and feed identifying leads that led to the arrest of two alleged members in Australia.

themes.theme: Scale and mechanics of the TeamPCP campaign

insights.claim: TeamPCP ran a repeating supply-chain attack cycle in 2026: compromise an open-source project, use it to steal developer credentials, then use those credentials to plant malware in the next widely used tool, cascading the breach outward.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: This repeating-cycle pattern is a template other supply-chain actors can copy; security teams should watch for credential-theft-then-repackage chains rather than one-off compromises.
insights.quote: It repeatedly compromised open-source software to hide its malware, which then allowed it to hijack the credentials of software developers and plant its malicious code in yet another widely used tool, in a repeating cycle.

insights.claim: TeamPCP's confirmed compromises in 2026 included the open-source security scanner Trivy, the AI API tool LiteLLM, infrastructure at web-app security firm Checkmarx, the web app library TanStack, and the enterprise AI platform Mistral AI, which cascaded into breaches of GitHub, data-contracting firm Mercor, and employee devices at OpenAI and the European Commission.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A concrete list of which widely-used dev-tool and AI-infra vendors were actually compromised — relevant for any portfolio exposure to these names' security posture and customer trust.
insights.quote: Starting this spring, for instance, TeamPCP compromised the open-source security scanner Trivy, the AI application programming interface tool LiteLLM, infrastructure of the web application security firm Checkmarx, the web app library TanStack, and the enterprise AI platform Mistral AI.

insights.claim: TeamPCP used a self-spreading worm nicknamed Mini Shai-Hulud (after the earlier September 2025 Shai-Hulud worm) to automate its supply-chain hacking and scale to more victims.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Automated, self-propagating supply-chain worms materially raise the blast radius and speed of a single upstream compromise — a structural risk for anyone dependent on open-source dependency chains.
insights.quote: At times, the group deployed a worm known as Mini Shai-Hulud, named after the sandworms in Dune, to automate its hacking and scale up to even more victims.

insights.claim: According to the Australian Federal Police, TeamPCP's haul included more than half a million users' stolen credentials, yet the group was only extracting tens of thousands of dollars in extortion payments — far below what comparable groups collect — which is why it began recruiting outside cybercriminal partners.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A large technical breach does not automatically translate into large financial extraction — monetization bottlenecks are themselves a security-economics signal worth tracking for threat-actor sophistication trends.

insights.claim: Google's security subsidiary Mandiant had an undercover analyst embedded inside TeamPCP's inner circle almost from the start of the group's public campaign, distinct from Google Threat Intelligence Group researcher Austin Larsen who presented the findings.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Shows Google/Mandiant is running active human-intelligence-style infiltration operations against cybercrime groups, not just passive telemetry analysis — a differentiator versus other threat-intel vendors.
insights.quote: “One of our personas had been working for many months to build trust with one of the actors that was invited to join TeamPCP, and so was added to the group,” Larsen told WIRED

insights.claim: Rather than notify each breached company individually, Google prioritized contacting the credential-hosting providers themselves (e.g., Amazon Web Services and Microsoft) to revoke stolen credentials at scale, judging that faster than reaching every victim directly.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A scalable disruption playbook — revoke at the platform layer rather than the victim layer — that other responders/vendors can replicate to cut response time on mass-credential-theft incidents.
insights.quote: Google first reached out to providers where those credentials could be used, like Amazon Web Services and Microsoft, to have the credentials revoked and prevent the hackers from exploiting them.

insights.claim: Google's visibility into TeamPCP's internal chat let it discover that a group member was using an AI tool to develop a zero-day exploit against widely used login software that would bypass its two-factor authentication; Google obtained and validated the exploit code, then warned the developer, who patched it.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A documented real-world case of an AI-assisted zero-day being created by a criminal group — concrete evidence that AI tooling is already lowering the bar for offensive exploit development, relevant to any AI-safety or cyber-insurance risk model.
insights.quote: someone within the group’s core circle was, distinct from the group’s supply-chain hacking, using an AI tool to develop a zero-day exploit in a widely used piece of login software that would allow the hackers to bypass its two-factor authentication

insights.claim: Larsen states Google's undercover analyst inside TeamPCP never engaged in or encouraged illegal hacking, staying passive enough only to avoid suspicion, under internal guardrails.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A legal/ethical boundary Google draws around its infiltration operations — relevant to how other corporate threat-intel teams might structure similar undercover programs without crossing into entrapment or complicity.
insights.quote: “They were a fly on the wall, only saying enough to not be suspicious,” Larsen says. “There are guardrails around what we do.”

insights.claim: The TeamPCP investigation coincided with the launch of Google's new Cyber Disruption Unit, which the company describes as tasked with a more aggressive, action-oriented approach to fighting cybercrime and state-sponsored hacking rather than only producing reports.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Signals a strategic shift at Google toward active disruption operations (credential revocation, infiltration) as a competitive/product differentiator in enterprise security, not just passive threat reporting.
insights.quote: “Google Threat Intelligence Group has put an emphasis on disruption. That’s one of our missions now,” Larsen says. “Writing reports can only be so useful. Taking action to protect users and customers—that is the next step.”

insights.claim: TeamPCP recruited outside cybercriminal groups, including the established extortion group ShinyHunters (known for the Canvas educational-platform breach), giving them access to stolen credentials in exchange for a cut of extortion proceeds, in an attempt to better monetize its haul.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Illustrates a criminal 'affiliate' monetization model — credential access shared for a revenue cut — mirroring legitimate SaaS partnership structures, useful context for understanding ransomware-as-a-service style economics.
insights.quote: TeamPCP invited multiple other cybercriminal groups to partner with it, giving them access to the stolen credentials in exchange for a percentage of any extortion payments they were able to extract.

insights.claim: ShinyHunters went rogue on its partnership with TeamPCP around April, using the shared stolen credentials to conduct its own extortions without paying TeamPCP its cut, then taunted TeamPCP publicly on X and unknowingly leaked TeamPCP's own internal chat logs to Google's analyst.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Shows criminal alliances are unstable and that infighting between threat actors can itself become an intelligence-gathering channel for defenders.
insights.quote: ShinyHunters went so far as to share with Larsen, unsolicited, a full log of the group’s chat on TeamPCP’s server—not knowing that he already had access via Google’s mole.

themes.theme: How the identification and arrest happened

insights.claim: Larsen traced an alleged TeamPCP leader's identity through old, unrelated forum data: a Gmail handle from a leaked BreachForums database led to a 2019 refund dispute referencing a PayPal account tied to a real name and email domain.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Demonstrates that years-old, seemingly unrelated leaked data (old forum disputes, old breach dumps) remains a primary deanonymization vector for threat actors — a durable pattern in cybercrime attribution work.
insights.quote: Larsen found in a leak of user data from the BreachForums hacker forum that one of the most active handles in the CanisterWorm chat had been registered with the Gmail address sheepstealing@gmail.com.

insights.claim: The decisive tip to the FBI came when Google observed that TeamPCP's newly moved stolen-credential server was being backed up to a Google Drive account tied to the same personal Gmail address already linked to the suspect, prompting Google to alert the FBI, which responded within minutes.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: A textbook operational-security failure (reusing a personal, identity-linked account for criminal infrastructure) was the single point of failure that unraveled the group — a recurring theme in cybercrime takedowns.
insights.quote: “When we saw that, I just thought: There’s no way. Why would he be sending all of this illicit, stolen material to a Google Drive that’s tied to himself?” Larsen says. “That’s when we gave the tip to the FBI.”
insights.locator: After TeamPCP moved its stolen credentials

insights.claim: About a month after Google's tip, two Australians in their early 20s, Ruben Ian Thomson and Louis Michael Gaebler, were arrested by Australian police working jointly with the FBI and charged as alleged principal participants in TeamPCP.
insights.speaker: WIRED
insights.so_what: Confirms real-world legal consequences followed the investigation, closing the loop on this specific threat-actor group.
insights.locator: About a month after his tip
